title: Video-Zero: Self-Evolution Video Understanding
claim: Prior approaches either need costly human labels or raise difficulty without grounding; ours generates evidence-centric, video-dependent questions that remain challenging.
layout: 3 columns left-to-right under a video frame strip; smiley/frown verdicts
description: A dashed banner across the top shows five video frames of a teal cup on a table. The cup tips over and shatters, frames numbered 1 to 5. Below, three columns are separated by dashed lines. Left, Traditional RL: an Annotator writes a question ("When does the cup drop?"), with checklist, money and clock icons, feeding a Solver. It is marked highly relevant but high cost. Middle, Traditional Self-Evolution: a Questioner with a difficulty slider (easy to hard) produces shallow questions such as "What color is the cup?", annotated common sense, shallow and single-frame. It is marked weakly relevant and only increasing difficulty. Right, Video-Zero: a Questioner with two sliders, video dependency and difficulty, asks "What changes happen to the cup?" It is marked highly relevant with deep reasoning. Orange frowns mark flaws and green smiles mark strengths. The eye goes first to the frames, then to the green and orange verdicts.
caption: Motivation and overview of Video-Zero. Traditional RL relies on costly labels; prior self-evolution often increases difficulty without explicit evidence focus. Video-Zero grounds question generation in evidence segments and co-evolves toward video-dependent, challenging supervision.
abstract: Self-evolution offers a promising path for improving reasoning models without relying on intensive human annotation. However, extending this paradigm to video understanding remains underexplored and challenging: videos are long, dynamic, and redundant, while the evidence needed for reasoning is often sparse and temporally localized. Naively generating difficult question-answer pairs from full videos can therefore produce supervision that appears challenging but is weakly grounded, relying on static cues or language priors rather than temporal evidence. In this work, we argue that the key bottleneck of video self-evolution is not difficulty alone, but grounding. We propose Video-Zero, an annotation-free Questioner--Solver co-evolution framework that centers self-evolution on temporally localized evidence. The Questioner discovers informative evidence segments and generates evidence-grounded questions, while the Solver learns to answer and align its predictions with the supporting evidence. This closes an iterative loop of evidence discovery, grounded supervision, and evidence-aligned learning. Across 13 benchmarks spanning temporal grounding, long-video understanding, and video reasoning, Video-Zero consistently improves multiple video VLM backbones, demonstrating the effectiveness and transferability of evidence-centered self-evolution.
